title: final Methods and Classes
summary: Lock classes against inheritance and lock methods against overriding to ensure design security and invariant stability.
learningOutcomes: Declare final classes to prevent inheritance completely (like java.lang.String)
Declare final methods to prevent subclasses from altering critical security algorithms
Understand the architectural rationale for locking designs against extension

activities.title: Practical Context: Locking Architectural Invariants for Security and Stability

analogy.story:
When a legal contract or will is finalized and signed by a judge, it is sealed with an official notarized wax stamp.

Nobody can subsequently append new pages to rewrite the clauses (Final Class: No inheritance / extension permitted). And nobody can cross out individual paragraphs or alter specific terms (Final Method: No overriding permitted).

A normal class is an open draft that other programmers can extend and override. A final class or method is that sealed legal document: its implementation is complete, finalized, and permanently protected against distortion.
analogy.takeaway: Marking a class final locks the entire blueprint against inheritance. Marking a method final locks its specific implementation against overriding.
analogy.headline: Everyday Analogy: The Sealed Legal Contract
analogy.keyTakeaway: Marking a class final locks the entire blueprint against inheritance. Marking a method final locks its specific implementation against overriding.

activities.content:
When creating foundational system classes (such as `String`, `Integer`, or security authenticators), designers must prevent malicious or poorly written subclasses from overriding core behavior.

If a third-party library could subclass `String` and alter string immutability, the security of the entire Java runtime would be compromised.

Declaring classes and methods as `final` guarantees architectural immutability and security.

activities.title: Final Methods and Final Classes: Definition, Security, and System Stability

concept.explanation:
Why would an engineer want to prevent other developers from extending their class or overriding their methods?

1. Security & Immutability (Final Classes):
   - Classic Example: java.lang.String.
   - If String were non-final, a malicious developer could extend String and create a subclass 'HackedString' that alters strings behind the scenes. Because file paths, network URLs, and usernames are stored in Strings, making String final guarantees system security.
   - Syntax: 'public final class SecurityKey { ... }'
   - Rule: A final class CANNOT be extended by any class ('class Sub inherits from SecurityKey' is a compile-time error).

2. Preserving Critical Algorithms (Final Methods):
   - If a class has a critical authentication or security hash calculation algorithm, marking the method 'final' allows other developers to inherit other features of the class, while strictly preventing them from overriding that critical method.
   - Syntax: 'public final boolean verifyCredentials(String token) { ... }'
   - Rule: Subclasses CAN inherit and call final methods, but CANNOT override them.
rules: Rule 1: If a class is declared final, all of its methods are implicitly final as well.
Rule 2: An incomplete base class can NEVER be declared final (they are exact opposites!).
Rule 3: Use final classes when designing value objects, security credentials, or utility toolkits.

questions.prompt: What happens if a developer attempts to extend a class marked as 'final' (e.g. class Sub inherits from FinalClass)?
questions.question: What happens if a developer attempts to extend a class marked as 'final' (e.g. class Sub inherits from FinalClass)?
options: The code compiles but throws an error at runtime
The compiler emits an error: 'cannot inherit from final ClassName'
The subclass is created as an interface
The final modifier is removed automatically
questions.explanation: Inheriting from a final class is strictly forbidden by the Java compiler.

questions.prompt: Why is java.lang.String declared as a 'final class' in the Java Standard Library?
questions.question: Why is java.lang.String declared as a 'final class' in the Java Standard Library?
options: To save 4 bytes of memory
For security, thread-safety, and performance: preventing malicious subclasses from altering string contents behind the scenes
Because Strings cannot store numbers
Because Strings are written in C++
questions.explanation: If String were open to inheritance, rogue subclasses could compromise file systems, network connections, and security credentials.

questions.prompt: Can an incomplete base class be declared as 'final' in Java (e.g. 'final incomplete base class Demo')?
questions.question: Can an incomplete base class be declared as 'final' in Java (e.g. 'final incomplete base class Demo')?
options: Yes, it is common practice
No, abstract and final are mutually contradictory: abstract REQUIRES inheritance, while final PREVENTS inheritance
Only if it contains static methods
Only in Java 17+
questions.explanation: 'abstract' demands subclasses, whereas 'final' forbids subclasses; using both together is a compile-time error.

questions.prompt: If a class is declared final, what is the default status of all methods inside that class?
questions.question: If a class is declared final, what is the default status of all methods inside that class?
options: All methods are automatically abstract
All methods are implicitly final (since no subclass can ever exist to override them)
All methods become static
All methods become private
questions.explanation: Because a final class cannot be extended, none of its methods can ever be overridden, making them implicitly final.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of marking an individual method 'final' in a non-final class?
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of marking an individual method 'final' in a non-final class?
options: To make the method run 100x faster
To lock that specific method's algorithm so subclasses cannot override or tamper with it
To prevent the method from taking parameters
To make the method return void
questions.explanation: A final method allows the class to be extended while protecting specific critical algorithms from modification.

questions.prompt: Can a final method be overloaded in the same class?
questions.question: Can a final method be overloaded in the same class?
options: No, final methods cannot be overloaded
Yes, overloading (different parameter signatures in the same class) is fully permitted on final methods
Only if the return type is int
Only if the method is static
questions.explanation: Overloading has nothing to do with overriding; final methods can be overloaded freely within the same class.

questions.prompt: In our legal contract analogy, what does the wax stamp preventing pages from being appended represent?
questions.question: In our legal contract analogy, what does the wax stamp preventing pages from being appended represent?
options: A final class that cannot be extended
A static block
A private variable
The compiler
questions.explanation: The sealed contract that cannot be extended represents a final class.

questions.prompt: Which of the following wrapper classes in java.lang is also declared final?
questions.question: Which of the following wrapper classes in java.lang is also declared final?
options: java.lang.Integer
java.lang.Double
java.lang.Boolean
All of the above
questions.explanation: All primitive wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Boolean, Long, etc.) are declared final to preserve immutable value semantics.

questions.prompt: Can a private method in a class be overridden by another class?
questions.question: Can a private method in a class be overridden by another class?
options: Yes, any method can be overridden
No, private methods are invisible to outside classes and subclasses, so they are implicitly final
Only if declared in the same file
Only in package-private classes
questions.explanation: Private methods cannot be seen by subclasses, so they can never be overridden (they are implicitly final).

questions.prompt: What compiler optimization does marking a method final enable (devirtualization)?
questions.question: What compiler optimization does marking a method final enable (devirtualization)?
options: The JVM can inline the method call directly because it knows the method cannot be overridden polymorphically at runtime
It converts the bytecode to C++
It deletes unused variables
It runs the code on the GPU
questions.explanation: The JVM JIT compiler can inline final methods safely without virtual method table dispatch overhead.

questions.question: Why would an API or library designer deliberately make a class final?
questions.answer: 1. Immutability guarantee: Prevents subclasses from adding mutable state or breaking value semantics (e.g. String, LocalDate). 2. Security: Prevents tampering with sensitive logic (like cryptography keys or credential validators). 3. Design simplicity: Follows Joshua Bloch's principle: 'Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it'.

questions.question: Can a final class contain non-final fields?
questions.answer: Yes! Marking a class final only prevents other classes from inheriting from it. It does not automatically make the class's fields final. Fields can still be mutable unless explicitly declared final.
keyTakeaways: Fields must be explicitly final for immutability

questions.question: What is JIT method inlining, and how do final methods facilitate it?
questions.answer: Normally, non-final instance methods require dynamic dispatch via the virtual method table (vtable). When a method is final, the JIT compiler knows definitively that no subclass overrides it, allowing it to eliminate the dispatch overhead and inline the method body directly into the caller's code.

questions.question: Can a constructor be declared final?
questions.answer: No. Constructors are never inherited by subclasses; each class has its own constructors. Because overriding constructors is impossible by definition, marking a constructor final is a syntax error.
keyTakeaways: Constructors are never inherited or overridden

questions.question: Why is 'abstract final' illegal on both classes and methods in Java?
questions.answer: 'abstract' means 'incomplete, must be extended/overridden'. 'final' means 'complete, cannot be extended/overridden'. They are polar opposites, so combining them causes an immediate compiler error.
keyTakeaways: abstract requires extension, final forbids it

questions.question: How does marking a class final impact testing frameworks like Mockito?
questions.answer: Historically, Mockito created dynamic subclasses at runtime to mock behavior; final classes could not be mocked without special bytecode plugins (like mockito-inline). Modern Mockito handles final classes transparently via instrumentation, but design-wise, composition is preferred over inheritance.
keyTakeaways: Modern Mockito handles via agent instrumentation

practiceProblems.title: Seal the Security Credential
practiceProblems.description:
Prevent class inheritance by sealing a security credential with the `final` keyword.

• Class `SecurityCredential`:
  - Declare as `final class SecurityCredential`
  - Field: `private final String apiKey;`
  - Constructor `SecurityCredential(String key)`: sets `this.apiKey = key;`
  - Getter: `public String getApiKey()`: returns `apiKey;`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `SecurityCredential cred = new SecurityCredential("API-SEC-99");`
  - Print: `Sealed API Key: [cred.getApiKey()]`

Target Console Output:
Sealed API Key: API-SEC-99

practiceProblems.title: Locked Password Hasher
practiceProblems.description:
Lock a critical security method using `final` so its implementation cannot be changed.

• Class `PasswordHasher`:
  - Method `public final String hashPassword(String raw)`:
    - If `raw == null`, returns `"HASHED_EMPTY"`
    - Otherwise, returns `"HASHED_" + raw`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `PasswordHasher hasher = new PasswordHasher();`
  - Print: `Result: [hasher.hashPassword("mypassword123")]`

Target Console Output:
Result: HASHED_mypassword123

practiceProblems.title: Sealed Immutable Point
practiceProblems.description:
Create a completely sealed coordinate record using both a `final` class and `final` fields.

• Class `ImmutableCoordinate`:
  - Declare as `final class ImmutableCoordinate`
  - Fields: `private final int x;`, `private final int y;`
  - Constructor `ImmutableCoordinate(int x, int y)`: sets both fields
  - Getters: `getX()`, `getY()`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `ImmutableCoordinate pt = new ImmutableCoordinate(10, 20);`
  - Print: `Coordinate: [[pt.getX()], [pt.getY()]]`

Target Console Output:
Coordinate: [10, 20]

practiceProblems.title: Fix Broken Code: Attempt to Override Final Method
practiceProblems.description:
Understand that final methods cannot be overridden; instead, callers simply invoke the verified implementation.

• Class `SecurityBase`:
  - Method: `public final boolean verifyChecksum(String token)`: returns `token != null && token.length() > 5`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `SecurityBase sec = new SecurityBase();`
  - Call `boolean valid = sec.verifyChecksum("SECURE_KEY");`
  - Print: `Checksum verified: [valid]`

Target Console Output:
Checksum verified: true

practiceProblems.title: Sealed License Key Validator
practiceProblems.description:
Seal an enterprise validation rule inside a `final class` with a `final` method.

• Class `LicenseKeyValidator`:
  - Declare as `final class LicenseKeyValidator`
  - Field: `private final String secretPrefix = "LIC-";`
  - Method `public final boolean isValidKey(String key)`:
    - Returns `true` if `key != null && key.startsWith(secretPrefix) && key.length() == 12`
    - Otherwise returns `false`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `LicenseKeyValidator validator = new LicenseKeyValidator();`
  - Test with key `"LIC-99887766"`
  - Print: `License valid: [validator.isValidKey("LIC-99887766")]`

Target Console Output:
License valid: true
